# Rate limiter — what it costs

<!-- Generated by persona/scripts/perf-ratelimit.ts. Do not edit by hand. -->

20,000 sequential `consume` calls per store, against Redis
running in Docker on the development machine. One call is what a limited
request pays before its handler runs.

| Store | p50 | **p95** | p99 | max | mean | calls/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Redis (deployed) | 0.140 | **0.193** | 0.266 | 21.498 | 0.148 | 6,749 |
| In process (fallback) | 0.000 | **0.000** | 0.001 | 0.303 | 0.000 | 3,101,677 |

All figures in milliseconds.

The Redis round trip adds **0.19 ms at p95** to a limited
request. The pre-registered threshold for `GET /oidc/me` is p95 < 200 ms, so
the limiter accounts for about 0.1% of the budget.

The in-process store is listed for contrast, not as an option: it is
per-process and empties on restart, so a deployment running on it would hand
an attacker a fresh budget on every deploy. `config.ts` refuses to start
production without `REDIS_URL` for that reason.

Both stores run the same token bucket at the same capacity — 120, the `oidcUserinfo` policy's, which is the hottest limited path. The in-process one runs the TypeScript in `token-bucket.ts`; Redis runs the Lua re-implementation of it in `redis.store.ts`, where the point of the script is that reading, refilling and taking a token are one atomic step.

The Redis tail is worth naming: p99 is 0.27 ms but the worst single
call was 21.5 ms. That is the connection warming up, not a
steady-state cost — it appears once, in the first handful of calls.
